chapter_theme: Trouble need not break a person: it can be laughed at, thought away, outlasted, or expected as the body's lot, until suffering itself seems to suffer. The chapter is a series of stances, not one remedy, and it closes the book's treatment of the king.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar sorts the chapter by source of trouble: fate (621-625), loss of wealth (626), and bodily strain (627-630). Manakkudavar maps it differently, taking 621-623 as general, 626 as loss of wealth, 627 as the hardship of austerity and 629 as the pain of desire; he ends the section on kingship at 630.

621.reading: When trouble comes, laugh; nothing else presses back on it as well.
621.nuance: The laugh is treated as a tactic, not a sign of being unaffected. Parimelazhagar says it borrows the joy of a finished task in the middle of the task, and that the lift it gives supplies the strength to push through.

622.reading: Even a flood of suffering is gone when a person of understanding merely thinks it through in the mind.
622.nuance: The verse doesn't say which thought. That gap is the whole dispute, and Pope's '(courageous)' fills it with one more answer.

positions.position: Suffering is nothing but a stance in the mind, and it vanishes when that stance is reversed.
The thought is that this is the fruit of one's deeds.
The thought is a practical one: how to defeat the trouble.
positions.quote: அதனை வெல்லும் வழி யாது என்பதை அறிவுடையவர்கள் நினைத்த மாத்திரத்திலேயே

623.reading: Those who do not suffer at suffering make suffering suffer.
623.nuance: The verse enacts its turn in four occurrences of one word. This reversal of subject and object recurs in 624 and 625, so the chapter's signature is grammatical. Parimelazhagar gives the mechanism: persisting finishes the task, and finishing ends all the troubles.

624.reading: Trouble that meets one who pulls through every obstruction like a draught ox itself has trouble.
624.nuance: Nothing about this image is heroic: Parimelazhagar cites Civakacintamani's picture of the ox on its side, nose to the ground. It sits beside the elephant of 597 and shows a humbler kind of strength.

625.reading: Though they come stacked one on another, the troubles of one who is not undone are themselves in trouble.

626.reading: Would those who never knew how to clutch at wealth, saying 'we have got it', grieve, saying 'we have lost it'?
626.nuance: Grief at losing is settled earlier, at the moment of having. The verse praises a lack of skill (தேற்றாதவர்), which is a wry way to describe a virtue.

627.reading: Knowing that the body is a target for suffering, they do not take trouble as a thing to be shaken by.

positions.position: மேல் means 'upon them', and the verse concerns bodies in all four states of birth, targets for a sword called suffering.
positions.quote: நாற்கதியினும் உள்ள உடம்புகள் இடும்பை என்னும் வாளுக்கு இலக்கு என்று தெளிந்து

positions.position: மேல் means 'the superior', and the context is the hardship taken on in austerity.
positions.quote: இது மேல் நன்மையாற் றவஞ் செய்யுங்கால் வருந் துன்பத்திற்கு அழியாதா ரைக் கூறிற்று.

628.reading: One who does not chase pleasure and calls suffering natural does not come to pain.
628.nuance: Pain is prevented by an expectation, not a defence. Parimelazhagar sees two conditions: wanting pleasure brings pain, and so does trying to ward off suffering as if it were not natural.

629.reading: One who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not feel the pain within pain.
629.nuance: The experience is not denied: the phrasing இன்பத்துள், துன்பத்துள் places a person within each. Parimelazhagar says they undergo them, yet do not desire or grieve, so that the deeds bear no fruit. That karmic consequence is his addition.

positions.position: Pleasure and pain here are those arising through work and effort, and both are held in the same way.
positions.quote: இரண்டையும் ஒரு தன்மையாகக் கோடலின், பயன்களும் இலவாயின.

positions.position: It concerns desire: one who doesn't lose himself in sensual pleasure isn't undone by the pain it brings.
positions.quote: இது காமத்தால் வரும் துன்பத்திற்கு அழியாதாரைக் கூறிற்று.

630.reading: If a person takes what hurts as pleasure, there comes to him a distinction even his enemies admire.
630.nuance: The reward is a rival's respect, which is the one kind that can't be flattery. Parimelazhagar's reason is philosophical: pain is no part of the self but a passing mental stance (கணிகம், momentary), which the verse does not claim.

links.note: Both use the phrase வெள்ளத் தனைய, 'as much as the flood'. In 595 the flood lifts a stalk, in a figure for the rise of energy. In 622 the flood is suffering itself, dissolved by a thought. In both the mind is what settles the scale.

Both refuse the cry over lost wealth. 593 says energy is the real asset, so the loss is small. 626 says the one who never clutched has no such cry. One rests on what you still have, and the other on how you first held it.

Both begin இன்பம் விழையான், 'not desiring pleasure'. In 615 this produces a pillar for kin through labour, and in 628 it produces a person pain can't reach. The same renunciation of pleasure serves worldly work and inner calm alike, without any talk of leaving the world.

Both ask for one response to good and bad, but they give different grounds: 379 reasons from fate that it's inconsistent to accept one and grieve the other, and 629 reasons from the training of desire, without mentioning fate.

source_issues: 621: Parimelazhagar's commentary is truncated at the start: the gloss before பிறிதில்லையாகலான் is missing.
